lines: Jordan Lee
+1 (555) 010-2468 | jordan.lee@example.com | example.com/code/jordan-lee
EDUCATION
Western State University | M.S. in Computer Engineering | Metro City, USA | Sep 2024 - Expected Jun 2026
Eastern Institute of Technology | B.S. in Electrical Engineering | Metro City, Country | Sep 2018 - Jun 2022
EXPERIENCE
Eastern Robotics Co. | Junior Software Engineer | Metro City, Country | Aug 2022 - Jul 2024
- Owned the diagnostics service's monitoring dashboards across two major releases and the on-call rotation that used them.
- Reduced p95 API latency from 420 ms to 180 ms by adding a request cache and batching sensor reads, with load tests that fail the build if p95 exceeds 200 ms.
- Maintained the CI pipeline for the perception team's model releases, adding automated regression checks that shortened release cycles from 2 weeks to 3 days.

- Migrated 30 robot-fleet services from cron jobs to an event queue while rewriting the shared logging library, onboarding two new hires and taking over the weekend on-call rotation, which removed the nightly backlogs that delayed morning dispatch.
Mobility Systems Company | Machine Learning Engineering Intern | Metro City, USA | Oct 2024 - May 2025

- Built a diagnostics triage branch for an industrial inspection system that screens 800+ sensor signals per case with ML-extracted features, cutting the pending-case backlog 68% in the eight weeks after launch.
- Raised diagnostic accuracy on 1,200 held-out cases from 71% to 79% by fine-tuning a domain adapter on validated tool-use trajectories with assistant-only loss masking.
- Cut p95 latency of single-request edge inference by 40% by serving the INT8 engine with dynamic batching.
- Using grouped tool-use rollouts, a composite reward over accuracy, citation validity and call count, and a GRPO loop with a frozen SFT reference, reduced end-to-end latency 5%.
- Stabilised GRPO training on sparse rewards by sampling a single rollout per prompt, so each update used exactly one scored trajectory.
- Documented the triage branch's abstention rules and escalation paths for the on-call reviewers, who adopted them as the team's runbook.
PROJECTS
Agent Runtime Suite | Owner | TypeScript, Multi-Agent Systems | Aug 2025 - Present
- Drove adoption of AI-first engineering practices across the platform, accelerating delivery and improving outcomes for downstream teams.
- Cut p95 tool-call latency from 900 ms to 600 ms, a 50% reduction, by caching tool results and reusing completed sub-agent answers.
- Raised the runtime's task-completion rate by 12% on the benchmark suite, from 71% to 83%, by retrying failed sub-agent calls with their partial context.
Research-Agent Evaluation Framework | Contributor | LLM Evaluation | Feb 2025 - Jul 2025
- Upstreamed 8 citation and faithfulness metrics to an open-source research-agent framework, where they now run in the default benchmark for every release.
- Showed the evaluator tracks injected degradation with a Kendall correlation of 0.89 across 400+ report-level trials that removed citations, sources and claims.
- Traced 3 structural pipeline defects in stability, sourcing and parameter handling to their modules with layered instrumentation; each was fixed upstream.
SKILLS
Programming: Python, TypeScript, Git
ML & Agents: PyTorch, LoRA, GRPO, agent evaluation, Kubernetes

items.says: Use consistent date and location formatting throughout.
Remove manual line breaks inside bullets and let the document editor wrap them naturally.
Avoid bullet wrapping that leaves short fragments such as “on-call,” “in,” or “on” alone.
items.because: Short fragments can make the résumé look poorly formatted.

items.says: Put Mobility Systems Company before Eastern Robotics Co.
items.because: The internship ended in May 2025, after the full-time role ended in July 2024.

items.says: Add a LinkedIn profile if it is complete and professional.
Make sure the code portfolio link is a direct, working URL.
Add a relevant graduate focus such as machine learning, distributed systems, robotics, or computer architecture if applicable.
Consider adding honors, a relevant concentration, or especially relevant courses if they strengthen the candidacy and space permits.
Clarify whether “owned” means design, implementation, alerting, maintenance, incident response, or operational responsibility.
items.because: Hiring managers need to see what the ownership involved.

items.says: Add scale such as the number of dashboards, services, users, incidents, or releases supported.
items.because: Hiring managers need to see what changed because of the work.

items.says: Reword “that used them” to remove ambiguity about whether it refers to the dashboards or the releases.
items.because: The reference is ambiguous.

items.says: Add an operational result such as reduced alert noise, faster incident response, or improved availability.
items.because: The bullet emphasizes responsibility rather than an outcome.

items.says: Clarify whether both caching and sensor-read batching caused the improvement or whether one was the primary cause.
items.because: The causal precision needs to be clearer.

items.says: Identify the affected API or service.
items.because: The bullet needs more contextual precision.

items.says: Identify the testing environment.
items.because: The bullet needs more contextual precision.

items.says: Clarify that the 200 ms threshold is a CI regression guard rather than a production SLO.
items.because: The safeguard’s context should be precise.

items.says: Specify whether the regression checks covered accuracy, latency, data quality, compatibility, or deployment validation.
items.because: The mechanism behind the result needs to be clearer.

items.says: Avoid implying that the regression checks alone shortened the release cycle unless that causal claim is defensible.
items.because: The causal mechanism needs to be clearer.

items.says: Clarify whether “release cycles” means time between releases, release preparation time, or time from commit to production.
items.because: The metric’s definition needs to be clearer.

items.says: Split the bullet or remove lower-priority details because it combines service migration, a logging rewrite, onboarding, and on-call responsibility.
items.because: The density makes the main accomplishment difficult to identify.

items.says: Clarify which action removed the nightly backlogs.
items.because: The causal relationship is unclear.

items.says: Quantify the backlog, dispatch-delay, duration, or failure-rate improvement.
items.because: The operational improvement is not quantified.

items.says: Explain whether the event-queue migration improved reliability, scalability, scheduling accuracy, or operational effort.
items.because: The significance of the migration is unclear.

items.says: Keep the onboarding detail only when mentorship or technical leadership is important to the target role.
items.because: It is a lower-priority detail in an already overloaded bullet.

items.says: Explain whether “triage branch” means a workflow, model path, service, or decision branch.
items.because: The system is not immediately understandable to an outside reader.

items.says: Clarify whether the overall system or the triage branch screens 800+ signals per case.
items.because: The current wording leaves the scope unclear.

items.says: Explain what the ML-extracted features contributed to the workflow.
items.because: The contribution is not immediately understandable.

items.says: Specify the baseline and measurement method for the 68% backlog reduction if space permits.
items.because: The result needs operational context.

items.says: Avoid implying that the launch alone caused the entire backlog reduction without a comparison period or operational context.
items.because: The causal claim needs more context.

items.says: Define “domain adapter” for audiences that are not strictly research-oriented.
items.because: The comparison needs enough context to be interpretable.

items.says: Clarify that the change from 71% to 79% is 8 percentage points, not an 8% relative increase.
items.because: The improvement should be expressed precisely.

items.says: State the baseline model or baseline training setup.
items.because: The comparison needs more evaluation context.

items.says: Identify the evaluation metric if accuracy could hide class imbalance or a multi-label setup.
items.because: The comparison needs to be interpretable.

items.says: Clarify how “single-request” inference benefited from dynamic batching.
items.because: Batching is usually associated with multiple requests.

items.says: Provide the before-and-after latency values if available.
items.because: The result needs more context.

items.says: Identify the inference engine or deployment environment if relevant.
items.because: The technical context is incomplete.

items.says: State the traffic load or hardware configuration under which the 40% reduction was measured.
items.because: The measurement conditions need to be clearer.

items.says: The sentence is a dependent introductory phrase without a clear subject.
items.because: The grammar obscures the accomplishment.

items.says: State what changed and what you personally implemented.
items.because: The technical details currently obscure the accomplishment.

items.says: Explain how the training procedure reduced end-to-end latency.
items.because: The causal connection is not obvious.

items.says: Define the comparison baseline for the 5% reduction.
items.because: The result needs clearer evaluation context.

items.says: Show whether the 5% result was statistically or operationally meaningful.
items.because: The significance of the result is unclear.

items.says: Remove implementation details that do not help explain the result.
items.because: The technical details currently obscure the accomplishment.

items.says: Distinguish full-workflow latency from the model or runtime latency in the preceding bullet.
items.because: The two latency claims may overlap or conflict.

items.says: Add an outcome such as fewer failed runs, lower variance, faster convergence, improved reward, or successful training completion.
items.because: The bullet describes a method rather than a result.

items.says: Explain why one rollout per prompt improved stability.
items.because: The mechanism may not be obvious to the intended audience.

items.says: Consider combining this bullet with the preceding one if both describe the same experiment.
items.because: The two bullets may overlap.

items.says: Quantify adoption or usage by reviewers, incidents, or operational cases.
items.because: The impact is currently limited to saying the runbook was adopted.

items.says: Clarify whether you created the runbook, standardized an existing process, or drove its adoption.
items.because: Your specific contribution is unclear.

items.says: Add an outcome such as fewer incorrect escalations, faster review, or more consistent handling.
items.because: The operational impact is not shown.

items.says: Replace the broad claim with a concrete technical contribution or measurable adoption result.
items.because: The bullet is generic, promotional, and unsupported by evidence.

items.says: Remove or substantially narrow “AI-first,” “accelerating delivery,” and “improving outcomes” unless supported by metrics.
items.because: These claims are overly promotional and unsupported.

items.says: State what you built, changed, or enabled and how many teams, users, or workflows were affected.
items.because: The bullet does not show a concrete contribution or scope.

items.says: Correct the claimed reduction from 50% to 33.3%, or correct the before-and-after values if 50% came from another measurement.
items.because: A drop from 900 ms to 600 ms is 33.3%, and the inconsistency can undermine confidence in the résumé.

items.says: Clarify whether the latency metric covers one tool call, a workflow, or all tool calls.
items.because: The metric’s scope is unclear.

items.says: Explain how cache invalidation, stale results, or correctness were handled if they were important constraints.
items.because: The relevant design constraints are not shown.

items.says: Describe the rise from 71% to 83% as 12 percentage points, not 12%, unless using the approximately 16.9% relative increase.
items.because: Percentage points and percentage increase must be precise.

items.says: Define whether task completion is measured per task, benchmark instance, or workflow.
items.because: The measurement unit is unclear.

items.says: Explain whether retries increased latency, cost, or tool calls if that tradeoff matters.
items.because: The approach may have relevant tradeoffs.

items.says: Identify the open-source framework by name if it is recognizable or publicly accessible.
items.because: Naming it would increase the contribution’s credibility.

items.says: Clarify whether you designed the metrics, implemented them, or both.
items.because: Your specific contribution is unclear.

items.says: Quantify the framework’s reach through users, repositories, releases, or benchmark runs if available.
items.because: Establishing adoption would increase credibility.

items.says: Verify that the metrics still run in the default benchmark for every release.
items.because: The claim must remain accurate and defensible.

items.says: Clarify whether the evaluator’s score was correlated with known degradation severity, a human ranking, or another reference.
items.because: The correlation is difficult to interpret without knowing the two variables.

items.says: Specify whether the statistic is Kendall’s tau.
items.because: The statistical measure should be precise.

items.says: Include statistical significance or confidence intervals if relevant.
items.because: The result needs enough statistical context to interpret.

items.says: Explain experimentally what it means to remove citations, sources, and claims.
items.because: The injected degradation procedure is unclear.

items.says: Distinguish whether the 400+ trials were independent reports, perturbations, or evaluation runs.
items.because: The trial unit is unclear.

items.says: Clarify whether stability, sourcing, and parameter handling are three separate defects or categories.
items.because: The defect structure is unclear.

items.says: Identify the practical impact of the fixes.
items.because: The reader needs to understand why the defects mattered.

items.says: Explain what “fixed upstream” means for audiences unfamiliar with the contribution workflow.
items.because: The project terminology may not be understood.

items.says: Git is categorized under “Programming” even though it is a version-control tool, not a programming language.
items.because: Skills should be organized so the technical profile is easy to scan.

items.says: Add technologies demonstrated in the experience section that you used directly and can discuss in an interview.
items.because: The current list does not reflect the breadth of the backend, systems, ML, and deployment work.

items.says: Separate frameworks, techniques, concepts, and platforms into clearer categories.
items.because: The skills section should make the technical profile easy to scan.

items.says: Represent relevant inference-serving, queueing, CI/CD, cloud, database, observability, testing, caching, and model-serving technologies actually used.
items.because: The current skills section makes the profile look narrower than the experience.

items.says: Place “agent evaluation” with evaluation or ML methods rather than treating it as a tool.
items.because: It is a capability area rather than a tool.

items.says: Add résumé evidence for Kubernetes use or remove it.
items.because: Kubernetes is not supported elsewhere in the résumé.
